text: Cassini's final plunge isn't about a dramatic finale. The main reason is that if it stayed in orbit, there's still a low chance of it eventually striking a moon. Enceladus is the big one because of its plumes and possible ocean, and we didn't want a long-dead spacecraft, or any Earth microbes on it, to contaminate a place that might be habitable. Crashing into Saturn's upper atmosphere means it gets destroyed and any debris gets pulled into the planet rather than wandering around the moon system. I think the neat part is that the whole thing was planned as a controlled end.

Most likely it’s not that the stationary leg is doing nothing; it’s actually doing a lot. When you ride, that leg has to hold your body over the board, absorb every bump, make tiny balance corrections, and keep your center of mass stable. Those small adjustments add up, especially if you’ve been pushing with the other leg almost all the time. The stationary leg gets fatigued and your hip, knee or ankle starts complaining, and that’s usually what people feel as pain. I know it feels counterintuitive because that leg looks like the resting one. But resting doesn’t mean unloaded; it’s loaded the whole time, and if your stance is too narrow or your knee caves inward, the stress concentrates on one side. A lot of skaters who push with one leg develop an imbalance that shows up as pain in the non-pushing leg. It can also be a sign you’re landing hard or not controlling the board with that leg, so it’s taking the shock instead of your core and arms. If the pain is in the knee or hip, check your form: keep the knee tracking over the toes, don’t let it cave in, and try to balance without gripping the deck so tightly. Switching which leg you push with helps too, because it keeps both legs and both hips working evenly. If you ride a lot, strengthening the stabilizer muscles, especially around the hip and knee, makes a big difference. You don’t need to turn every ride into a workout, but a few minutes of side lunges or bodyweight squats can make the stationary leg less likely to hurt. For now I’d treat it as a signal that the non-pushing leg is doing more stabilizing work than you’re giving it credit for.

It's mostly about ancestry, not where someone was born. The term African American means a person in America who traces some part of their heritage to Africa. Most Black Americans weren't born in Africa, but many of their families were brought there centuries ago, and the name points to that origin. So the -American part locates them in the USA, while the Afro/African part marks the ancestral connection. It's not a claim that most currently live in Africa or recently moved there. Some Black Americans may have mixed roots, or family connections to the Caribbean or elsewhere, but the label still uses Africa as the broad geographic reference point. In everyday usage it's shorthand for Black people with African descent, much like calling someone an Asian American because of family heritage rather than where they stand in the world. The question assumes the label means literal residence. It doesn't. Afro-American was also used as a way to reclaim identity in America. Some people prefer African American or just Black, but the key point remains: it names the continent of origin, not the current country. That's why the wording can feel odd if you think of African as a nationality or current home.

tbh there isn't one source. Historically, many groups got weapons through state backers, and the foreign involvement has kept changing, so what one side gets can flip depending on who's fighting who. Local production and captured arms also matter, and there's always some grey-market flow from neighbours. As for why they keep getting them, factions still need to defend themselves, their rivals are doing the same, and external powers see arms as leverage. Once you're in a long war, the logistics of keeping units armed becomes routine, not a one-off thing, and that's what keeps the pipeline open.

I only saw the subject line, A few questions on house-buying stuff, so I'm answering the general bit rather than the specific questions you may have had. My take is that buying a home is mostly about cash flow, not romance. The interesting part for me is how the purchase has to live with your life now, not just the dream of it. You can afford a mortgage number on paper but still get squeezed if you have a small job or unexpected costs. I think you should look at the running costs too, taxes, insurance, maintenance, and whatever the HOA or building fees are. A pretty cheap property can still trap you in a high cost area, and a small monthly bill can add up fast. If the premise was that you wanted specific answers, I didn't see them. So treat this as a first pass. If you send the actual list, I'll give a more direct answer. I'd also check what your own savings could cover if income stopped, and how quickly the market moves where you're looking. I'm pretty sure you should get the numbers checked by someone who does this for a living.

Good question. The short version is that scientists don't watch a coastline disappear. They use very precise positioning systems, especially GPS, to track stations on the continents over years. By comparing the coordinates today with those from previous years, they can tell how far and which direction a spot has moved.

GPS isn't just for cars, and the same basic idea also shows up in satellite geodesy, very long baseline radio astronomy, and laser ranging. The numbers are tiny, a few centimetres a year, but over long periods those tiny shifts become large. So a continent isn't visibly sliding past a fixed landmark. We measure the change in position of many points, fit a model, and infer the motion.

It's a little like tracking a slow ship from a fixed port, except the port is also on moving ground, so you have to be very careful about what you're using as reference.

Inbreeding makes relatives more likely to carry the same rare harmful genes, so children are more likely to have two copies of a bad recessive mutation. That’s the main science bit. It doesn’t usually create new damage, it just increases homozygosity, the chance that two copies of the same variant line up. Many of these variants affect brain development or overall health, and because they’re rare in the wider population, relatives are a good source for matching them. So you get a higher genetic load, and that can show up in cognition, not just one simple dumb gene. The effect is statistical, not a fixed rule, and the size depends on how closely related the parents are.

tbh the word IQ here is a proxy for broader cognitive impact. Pretty sure the key point is that inbreeding uncovers hidden recessive problems rather than manufacturing new ones, in general, across traits.

Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it interferes with the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Red blood cells normally use hemoglobin to transport oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues. Hemoglobin has a very strong attraction to carbon monoxide, much stronger than its attraction to oxygen. In simple terms, CO does not need to reach high levels to cause harm, because even a small amount can occupy many hemoglobin sites and leave less room for oxygen. It also changes how hemoglobin releases oxygen, so tissues get less even where oxygen is present. This reduces oxygen delivery to organs such as the brain and heart, which is why even modest exposure can produce headache, dizziness, confusion, or worse. Because it is colorless, odorless, and tasteless, people can absorb it before noticing. That is why CO poisoning can be so deceptive.

Carbon dioxide is different. It is a normal waste product of metabolism, and the lungs remove it continuously. At everyday concentrations it is not considered poisonous in the same way as CO. The body can tolerate a wide range of CO2 levels, and the respiratory system adjusts breathing to keep it within normal bounds. High CO2 can still be harmful if ventilation is poor, but its danger comes more from its abundance and acid-base effects rather than from blocking oxygen transport. CO, by contrast, is a nearly invisible, odorless gas that binds hemoglobin tightly and prevents oxygen from being picked up or released properly.

For a new colleague, the key distinction is this. CO2 is something we produce and expel. CO is something we can accidentally inhale from incomplete combustion, and once in the bloodstream it quietly reduces oxygen availability. That is why CO is a major hazard in enclosed spaces, and why detectors are used to catch it before symptoms become serious.

The brace position is a protective posture that passengers and crew are taught for sudden stops, hard landings, or impacts. It works by bringing your body into a stable shape, keeping your head, neck and torso supported so they are less likely to be thrown forward or sideways. If you are seated, you lower your head toward your knees, keep your back against the seat, and wrap your arms around your legs. This does not make the aircraft safe, but it can reduce the chance of serious injury.

In an impact, your body has momentum and would normally slam into the seatback, tray table, or overhead bins. The brace limits that motion. It also helps keep your head from striking your knees or the seat, and it protects your chest, back, and limbs from hitting hard surfaces. For a new colleague, the key idea is simple: the position turns you into a more compact and supported shape, and that smaller, more controlled movement is what reduces the risk of fractures and head injuries. In real emergencies, a trained crew will call out and guide you into the position, so the value is in following the cue quickly rather than guessing.

Age alone does not guarantee survival or recognition. Many pre-industrial companies were small local concerns, family businesses, guilds, or trade routes that left thin records, so later generations have little to point to. Factories, mass production, and advertising changed what a famous business looks like. Older firms were often absorbed, renamed, or faded away. In practice, a few ancient businesses still exist, but most were not famous in the way we usually think of brands. If you cannot name many, it is less that none existed and more that fame, records, and scale are usually products of the industrial and consumer era.

To me, the human body doesn't produce electricity the way a battery does; it generates it on demand through chemical signals. My position is that it's fundamentally about ion movement. Every cell has a membrane that acts like a selective gate. When a nerve fires, sodium channels open, flooding the cell with positive charge, and then potassium channels follow to restore balance. This rapid swap of ions is what we call an action potential. It's not a steady current, but a wave of tiny voltage changes that zip down the nerve to tell muscles to contract. So the "electricity" is just chemistry in motion.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, and afterward I learned it actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

I'm keeping it, four stars. The space bar rattles, and when you hit it with the edge of your thumb it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key repeats on occasion, so example gets typed as eexample and I have to backspace. That happens maybe once an afternoon, usually when I'm typing fast and not looking. I paid $38 and kept it anyway because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I'd already pulled off a keycap and found out myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard. My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.
